clinicalPearls: One of the commonest congenital anomalies of the spleen, resulting from failure of fusion of the multiple splenic buds that arise in the dorsal mesogastrium; the tissue is histologically identical to normal spleen with its own capsule and splenic-artery blood supply
Most lie at or near the splenic hilum, but they also occur along the splenic vessels, in the tail of the pancreas, the gastrosplenic and splenocolic ligaments and, rarely, the pelvis or scrotum

Usually an asymptomatic incidental finding that enhances identically to the spleen on every imaging phase, which is the key to distinguishing it from lymphadenopathy, an adrenal nodule or a pancreatic tail neoplasm

A residual or hypertrophied accessory spleen is an important cause of persistent or recurrent cytopenia after splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia or hereditary spherocytosis, so accessory tissue must be actively sought and removed at operation
An intrapancreatic accessory spleen in the tail closely mimics a hypervascular neuroendocrine tumour and is a classic radiological pitfall

Splenic tissue can be confirmed non-invasively with technetium-labelled heat-damaged red cell or sulphur colloid scintigraphy (ideally with SPECT/CT) or with superparamagnetic iron oxide MRI, avoiding unnecessary surgery
Rarely a pedunculated accessory spleen undergoes torsion, infarction or spontaneous rupture and presents as an acute abdomen
reference.pathophysiology: Accessory spleens arise when the several splenic primordia that develop within the dorsal mesogastrium during embryogenesis fail to coalesce into a single organ, leaving one or more discrete nodules of splenic tissue. Each nodule is invested by its own capsule and is supplied by branches of the splenic artery, and it is histologically and functionally indistinguishable from the main spleen, performing the same filtering, immune and, when demanded, haematopoietic roles. Because the tissue is genuine splenic parenchyma it can hypertrophy when the orthotopic spleen is diseased or has been removed, which underlies relapse of haematological disease after splenectomy.
additionalDifferentials: Pancreatic tail neuroendocrine tumour or other pancreatic mass (intrapancreatic type)
Splenosis (acquired autotransplanted splenic implants after trauma or splenectomy)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI demonstrating enhancement paralleling that of the spleen on all phases
Technetium-labelled heat-damaged autologous red cell or sulphur colloid scintigraphy with SPECT/CT to confirm functioning splenic tissue
Superparamagnetic iron oxide-enhanced MRI for problem-solving, particularly the intrapancreatic type
Ultrasound with Doppler showing an echotexture matching the spleen and a splenic-artery pedicle
Blood film for Howell-Jolly bodies after splenectomy, whose absence suggests persistent functioning splenic tissue
Cross-sectional localisation imaging when relapse of immune thrombocytopenia raises suspicion of a missed accessory spleen
redFlags: Acute abdomen from torsion, infarction or spontaneous rupture of a pedunculated accessory spleen
Recurrent or persistent cytopenia after splenectomy suggesting a missed or hypertrophied accessory spleen
A lesion mistaken for malignancy leading to unnecessary major surgery
Haemodynamic compromise from haemorrhage of a ruptured splenule
reference.prognosis: Accessory spleens are benign and carry an excellent prognosis, becoming clinically relevant only when they undergo torsion, mimic a neoplasm, or hypertrophy and cause relapse of a haematological disorder after splenectomy. Recognition on imaging usually spares the patient unnecessary intervention.
pitfalls: Mistaking an accessory spleen for a pancreatic tail neoplasm, adrenal mass or lymph node and proceeding to unnecessary biopsy or resection
Failing to search for and remove accessory splenic tissue during splenectomy for immune or haemolytic disease, leading to relapse
Not recognising retained splenic function (absent Howell-Jolly bodies) as a clue to residual splenic tissue
Confusing an accessory spleen with acquired splenosis or with polysplenia of heterotaxy
Overlooking accessory tissue on pre-operative imaging
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
management: For an asymptomatic incidental accessory spleen, no treatment is needed beyond confirming its splenic nature and avoiding unnecessary intervention

Confirm splenic tissue non-invasively with technetium-labelled heat-damaged red-cell or sulphur-colloid scintigraphy with SPECT/CT, or superparamagnetic iron oxide MRI, to distinguish it from a neoplasm and prevent needless surgery
At splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia or hereditary spherocytosis, actively seek and excise accessory splenic tissue to prevent disease relapse
For persistent or recurrent cytopenia after splenectomy, localise and remove a residual or hypertrophied accessory spleen by completion splenectomy
Surgical excision for a symptomatic accessory spleen complicated by torsion or infarction presenting as an acute abdomen
Provide post-splenectomy infection prophylaxis with immunisation against encapsulated organisms and antibiotic prophylaxis where functioning splenic tissue is removed
